details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Scaling up the existing system by creating 500 individual per-model dashboards.
**The Rationale:** Engineers lean on their experience with microservices, assuming every deployed artifact needs its own granular glass pane.
**The Consequence:** Massive alert fatigue. Dashboards are ignored, critical failures are lost in the noise, and on-call engineers burn out.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Fleet size: 500 models.
   - Option A (Dashboards): 1 per model.
   - Option B (Anomaly): 1 fleet view, ~5-10 statistical alerts/day.
   - Option C (SLOs): 3-4 Tiers, alerts only on burn rate.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Option A overhead: 500 dashboards = 100% guarantee of alert fatigue and unmanageable maintenance.
   - Option C (SLOs) alerts: ~10-15 highly actionable, severity-mapped alerts per day across the entire fleet.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: SLOs + Error Budgets.** The operations team is **Human-Attention-Bound**; error budgets mathematically restrict alerts to genuine SLA-threatening events.
details.realistic_solution: Implement SLO-based monitoring with error budgets as the primary framework, augmented with fleet-wide anomaly detection. Group the 500 models into 3-4 criticality tiers (e.g., Tier 1: 99.9% accuracy). Track error budget burn rates; if a model burns >50% of its budget in 24 hours, it triggers an actionable alert. This completely eliminates alert noise from healthy models. Anomaly detection provides a secondary catch-all for unknown-unknowns without requiring manual threshold tuning.

question: How would you design monitoring for 500 models, and which of per-model dashboards, anomaly detection, or SLOs should be primary?
scenario: Your platform grew from 10 to 500 models. The existing flat monitoring (all metrics in one dashboard) is unusable, creating too many alerts and no clear escalation path.
title: Monitoring Architecture for Multi-Model Fleet

book_refs.title: Model Serving
book_refs.why: Inference servers, autoscaling, cold start are the model-serving chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Solving missed incidents by adding more alerts or stricter thresholds.
**The Rationale:** Believing that capturing every possible deviation ensures reliability.
**The Consequence:** Worsens the signal-to-noise ratio, exacerbating alert fatigue and leading to total operational failure.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- 200 alerts/day with a 95% false positive rate.
- Operator bandwidth: ~20 alerts investigated/day.

**Calculations:**
- True alerts: 200 × 0.05 = 10 real alerts.
- False alerts: 200 × 0.95 = 190 noise alerts.
- Investigation capacity vs total alerts: 20 / 200 = 10% coverage.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Operational-Bound**. Because operators can only process 10% of the volume, the 10 real alerts are statistically buried in the 190 noise alerts, guaranteeing missed incidents.
details.realistic_solution: Alert fatigue occurs when operators receive so many alerts that they become desensitized and stop responding — even to critical ones. ML systems are especially vulnerable because: (1) ML metrics are inherently noisy — accuracy fluctuates batch-to-batch, latency spikes with traffic patterns, and data quality varies daily. Static thresholds on noisy metrics generate excessive false alarms. (2) ML systems have more failure modes than traditional software — data drift, feature staleness, model degradation, concept drift — each with its own metrics and thresholds. (3) Multi-model platforms multiply the problem: 50 models × 4 alert rules each = 200 potential alerts. When operators ignore 95% of alerts (because they are false positives), they inevitably miss the 5% that matter. The 12-hour missed incident is the classic consequence — the critical alert was buried in noise.

question: What is alert fatigue, and why did 200+ daily alerts make the 12-hour missed ML degradation likely?
scenario: Your ML platform generates 200+ alerts per day across 50 models. The on-call team acknowledges but ignores most of them. Last week, a critical model degradation was missed for 12 hours despite being alerted. You need to explain what alert fatigue is and why it is especially dangerous for ML systems.
title: Alert Fatigue in ML Systems

book_refs.title: Model Serving
book_refs.why: Inference servers, autoscaling, cold start are the model-serving chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Calculating the reduction only on total overall alerts.
**The Rationale:** Candidates apply the FP reduction globally, forgetting 2 rules are unchanged.
**The Consequence:** Inaccurate estimates undermine trust in observability improvements.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- 200 total alerts. Noisy rules = 160 alerts (90% FP).
- Unchanged rules = 40 alerts.
- New FP rate for noisy rules = 20%.

**Calculations:**
- Old True Alerts (Noisy): 160 * (1 - 0.90) = 16.
- New Noisy Total: True alerts (16) must be 80% of total. 16 / 0.8 = 20.
- New Total Alerts: 20 (noisy) + 40 (unchanged) = 60.
- Reduction: 200 - 60 = 140.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 140 alerts reduced (Signal-Bound)**. False positives drop drastically while retaining all 16 true anomalies.
details.realistic_solution: Current state: 160 alerts from noisy rules. At 90% FP, 16 are true and 144 are false. After anomaly detection (20% FP), the 16 true alerts represent 80% of total noisy alerts. New noisy alerts = 16 / 0.8 = 20. Non-noisy rules remain at 40. Total = 60. Reduction = 140.

question: How many of the 200 daily alerts are reduced by moving the 3 noisy rules that generate 80% of alerts to anomaly detection?
scenario: You have 50 models with 5 alert rules. 80% of the 200 daily alerts come from 3 noisy rules with a 90% false positive rate. You switch these 3 rules to anomaly detection, cutting their FP rate to 20%.
title: Daily Alert Reduction From Noisy Rule Anomaly Detection

book_refs.title: Network Architectures
book_refs.why: NAS is architectural; hardware-aware/MCUNet-style search is an edge topic.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Focusing heavily on the search algorithm (RL, evolutionary) while using an overly broad search space.
**The Rationale:** Candidates assume a smart algorithm can efficiently navigate any space, ignoring that a bad search space is computationally intractable and lacks implicit priors.
**The Consequence:** Millions of wasted GPU hours searching an intractable space without finding a better architecture.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Naive NAS: 10,000 architectures at 10 GPU-hours each.
- Weight-sharing NAS: 1 supernet at 1,000 GPU-hours + 10 GPU-hours search.

**Calculations:**
- Naive search cost: 10,000 * 10 = 100,000 GPU-hours.
- Weight-sharing cost: 1,000 + 10 = 1,010 GPU-hours.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Compute Search Bound**. Weight-sharing reduces the computational cost by ~100x compared to naive search.
details.realistic_solution: NAS automates architecture design by searching over a defined operation space. The search space defines what architectures are possible: which operations (convolutions, attention, pooling), which connections (skip connections, dense connections), and which hyperparameters (width, depth, kernel size). Search space design matters most because: (1) too broad a space is computationally intractable (10^18 possible architectures), (2) too narrow misses good designs, (3) the space implicitly encodes your priors about what works. NAS is expensive because evaluating each candidate requires training it (or a proxy) to estimate performance. Early NAS methods (Zoph & Le, 2017) used 800 GPUs for 28 days. Modern approaches reduce cost through weight sharing (supernet training), performance predictors, and hardware-aware constraints that prune the space. But even efficient NAS costs 100-1000x more than training a single model.

question: Why does NAS search-space design matter more than the search algorithm, and why is NAS so computationally expensive?
scenario: A colleague proposes using NAS to find the optimal model architecture for your edge deployment.
title: NAS Search Space and Cost

book_refs.title: Network Architectures
book_refs.why: NAS is architectural; hardware-aware/MCUNet-style search is an edge topic.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Forgetting that supernet training is the dominant cost of the entire procedure.
**The Rationale:** Candidates focus intensely on the evolutionary search phase because "evaluating 500 networks" sounds incredibly expensive.
**The Consequence:** They fail to realize the architecture search itself is extremely cheap, leading to incorrect capacity/cost estimation.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Supernet training: 8 GPUs × 24 hours.
- NAS Evaluation: 500 sub-networks at 2 min/eval.
- Cost: $3 / GPU-hour.

**Calculations:**
- Supernet GPU-hours: 8 × 24 = 192 GPU-hours.
- Eval GPU-hours: 500 × 2 min = 1000 min = 16.67 GPU-hours.
- Total GPU-hours: 192 + 16.67 = 208.67 GPU-hours.
- Total Cost: 208.67 × $3/hour = $626.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 208.7 GPU-hours costing $626. Supernet training dominates (92% of budget) (Compute-Bound)**.
details.realistic_solution: Supernet training: 8 GPUs × 24 hours = 192 GPU-hours. Architecture search: 500 evaluations × 2 min = 1000 min ≈ 16.7 hours on 1 GPU = 16.7 GPU-hours. If parallelized across 8 GPUs: 16.7/8 ≈ 2.1 hours wall time. Total GPU-hours: 192 + 16.7 = 208.7 GPU-hours. Cost: 208.7 × $3 = $626. For comparison, training a single architecture manually: ~24 GPU-hours ($72). NAS costs ~8.7x more than a single training run but explores 500 architectures. If the NAS-found architecture is even 10% more efficient at inference, it saves far more than $626 over the model's deployment lifetime. The 192 GPU-hours for supernet training dominates (92% of total cost).

question: What are the total GPU-hours and dollar cost of this weight-sharing NAS run at $3 per GPU-hour?
scenario: You run a weight-sharing NAS for an edge vision model. The supernet trains for 200 epochs on 8 GPUs (takes 24 hours). Training a single derived architecture from scratch takes 24 GPU-hours. The evolutionary search evaluates 500 sub-networks (each evaluation takes 2 minutes on 1 GPU).
title: NAS Compute Budget

book_refs.title: Network Architectures
book_refs.why: NAS is architectural; hardware-aware/MCUNet-style search is an edge topic.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Automatically selecting NAS because it sounds mathematically rigorous and state-of-the-art.
**The Rationale:** Candidates ignore the massive engineering setup time and risk associated with running a custom NAS search.
**The Consequence:** Wasting the entire 2-week budget on infrastructure setup and failing to deliver a working model.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - 2 weeks, 1000 GPU-hours.
   - NAS: 5 days setup, 200 GPU-hours search, 800 GPU-hours training.
   - Adapt: 2 days setup, 1000 GPU-hours training.
2. **Calculations:**
   - NAS total time: 5 days setup + (1000 GPU-hours / cluster capacity). High risk of >14 days.
   - Option B: Fits easily in timeline, gives 90% NAS quality.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   **Result: Time Bound. Option B provides 90% quality with 20% risk, making it the only safe choice.**
details.realistic_solution: Option B (adapt existing architectures) is optimal. Proven architecture families get you 90% of NAS quality at 20% of the engineering effort. NAS setup takes too long, and pretrained models may not meet strict latency.

question: With 2 weeks, 1000 GPU-hours, and a 200ms edge latency limit, which model-selection option would you choose and why?
scenario: Your team has 2 weeks and 1000 GPU-hours to find the best model for an edge device with a 200ms latency constraint. Options: (A) hardware-aware NAS, (B) manually adapt existing architectures, (C) use a pretrained model zoo and fine-tune.
title: NAS vs Manual Design

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Blaming the model for intentionally being biased.
**The Rationale:** Candidates assume the model architecture is flawed, rather than realizing the model is correctly optimizing for the metric based on causally constrained data.
**The Consequence:** Attempting to tweak model hyperparameters rather than fixing the endogenous training data distribution.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Two content types: A and B.
- The model gives more exposure to content with higher observed engagement.
- Training data comes only from shown items, so exposure controls what future data exists.

**Calculations:**
- If type A receives 60% of exposure, roughly 60% of observed engagement data comes from type A even if unshown type B items might have performed well.
- Retraining on that biased log teaches the model that type A has more evidence and lower uncertainty.
- The next policy shifts still more exposure to type A, causing the logged dataset to become increasingly type-A-heavy.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Data Distribution-Bound.** The issue is not a computed convergence rate; it is that model-generated exposure creates the next training distribution, systematically eroding content diversity.
details.realistic_solution: A feedback loop forms when: (1) the model recommends content based on predicted engagement, (2) users can only engage with content they are shown (selection bias), (3) the model is retrained on this engagement data, which overrepresents the types of content the model already promotes. Each retraining cycle amplifies the bias: popular content types get more exposure → more engagement data → higher predicted engagement → even more exposure. This creates a positive feedback loop that converges toward a narrow content distribution (filter bubble). Content that was never shown has zero engagement data, so the model never learns to recommend it — even if users would have liked it. The fundamental issue is that the training distribution is not independent of the model — it is endogenous, violating the standard ML assumption of i.i.d. training data.

question: How did the recommender's training feedback loop form, and why does it produce filter bubbles?
scenario: A content recommendation model is retrained on user engagement data (clicks, watch time). Over 6 months, the content mix becomes increasingly homogeneous.
title: Recommender Feedback Loops and Filter Bubbles

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Choosing demographic parity alone.
**The Rationale:** It directly addresses the final output distribution, which seems like the quickest and easiest regulatory fix.
**The Consequence:** The model fights against the constraint since the underlying training data remains biased, ultimately reducing overall accuracy without addressing the root cause.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Goal: Break the bias feedback loop in regulated lending.
   - Constraints: Ethical/legal compliance, outcome fairness, predictive accuracy.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Exploration (A): Can collect missing outcome data, but random approvals or denials create serious legal, ethical, and borrower-harm risks.
   - Causal Inference (B): Directly targets selection bias in historical approvals, but depends on overlap, measured confounders, and auditability of assumptions.
   - Demographic Parity (C): Provides an output-level fairness guardrail, but does not repair the biased repayment labels and can reduce accuracy if used alone.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: Use B as the primary mitigation with C as a monitored safety constraint.** Exploration is only appropriate under carefully governed pilots, not as the default mechanism for high-stakes lending.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (exploration/random approval): Most direct way to get unbiased outcome data. But ethically and legally problematic: randomly approving loans creates financial risk for both lender and borrowers who may not be ready. Also, random denial of qualified applicants is discriminatory. Feasibility: low in regulated domains. Option B (causal inference): Use techniques like inverse propensity weighting to account for the selection bias in historical data. Estimate what the repayment rate would have been if the denial had not occurred. Does not require experimentation on real people. Limitation: requires strong causal assumptions and sufficient overlap in the data. Option C (demographic parity): Ensures equal approval rates across groups but may approve genuinely high-risk applicants (increasing defaults) or deny genuinely low-risk applicants from the majority group. Treats the symptom, not the cause. Recommendation: B as the primary approach (debias the data), augmented with C as a safety constraint (ensure outputs are not discriminatory while causal estimates are imperfect). A is inappropriate for high-stakes lending decisions.

question: How would you evaluate exploration, causal debiasing, and demographic parity for mitigating the lending feedback loop?
scenario: Your lending model trained on historical approval data has a feedback loop: it denies loans to a demographic group, leading to no repayment data for that group, causing the model to learn the group is high-risk, and denying more loans.
title: Lending Feedback Loop Fairness Mitigation

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Relying solely on the system prompt to enforce guardrails.
**The Rationale:** Engineers assume modern LLMs will strictly follow instruction constraints within their context window.
**The Consequence:** The system is easily bypassed by prompt injection, exposing the company to legal and reputational risk.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- System Prompt Only compliance rate: ~70%.

**Calculations:**
- + Input Guardrail: Increases to ~90%.
- + Output Guardrail: Increases to ~98%.
- + Deterministic Filters: Increases to ~99.5%.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 99.5% Compliance (Reliability-Bound)**. Defense in depth is essential to reach acceptable enterprise compliance levels.
details.realistic_solution: LLM guardrails are defense layers at multiple points in the inference pipeline: (1) Input guardrails (pre-model): classify incoming prompts before they reach the LLM. A semantic router or topic classifier detects off-topic requests (medical queries, pricing probes). Blocks or redirects before the LLM even sees the prompt. Fast and cheap. (2) Output guardrails (post-model): scan the LLM's response before returning to the user. A secondary classifier checks for medical claims, pricing information leaks, or policy violations. Can rewrite, redact, or block the response. (3) Deterministic filters: regex/keyword filters for known-bad patterns (credit card numbers, internal URLs, specific banned phrases). Zero false negatives for exact matches. (4) Semantic filters: lightweight classifier models that detect intent categories (medical advice, financial advice) even when phrased creatively. All four layers work together — no single layer is sufficient because each catches different attack vectors.

question: What guardrails would prevent medical advice, pricing leaks, and off-topic replies, and where do they sit in the pipeline?
scenario: Your company is deploying an LLM-based customer service chatbot. The legal team requires that the bot never gives medical advice, never discloses internal pricing logic, and always stays on-topic.
title: Guardrail Architecture Layers

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming all safety guardrails must execute strictly sequentially after generation completes.
**The Rationale:** Candidates mentally separate "generation" and "moderation" into rigid phases, forgetting that token streaming allows for powerful temporal overlap.
**The Consequence:** The system incurs massive, unnecessary latency, leading to degraded user experience or failure to accommodate future safety models.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Budget: 2000ms.
- Current Inference: 1200ms.
- Guardrails: Input (150ms), Output (200ms), Regex (5ms).

**Calculations:**
- Sequential Pipeline = 150ms + 1200ms + 200ms + 5ms = 1555ms.
- Optimized (Streaming) = Output classifier processes asynchronously. Finishes ~20ms after final token.
- Optimized Time = 150ms + 1200ms + 20ms = 1370ms.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 1370ms (Latency-Bound)**. Streaming architecture saves 185ms by overlapping moderation with generation, leaving a 630ms buffer for future features.
details.realistic_solution: A sequential pipeline fits, but with streaming output, the output classifier can process tokens as they are generated, overlapping with LLM inference. This heavily optimizes the pipeline.

question: Do the input/output classifiers and regex filter fit within the 2-second chatbot latency budget, and how can you optimize them?
scenario: Your LLM chatbot has a 2-second total latency budget. The LLM inference takes 1.2 seconds. You need to add an input classifier (150ms), output classifier (200ms), and regex filter (5ms).
title: Guardrail Latency Budget

book_refs.title: ML Operations
book_refs.why: Data/concept drift and training-serving skew are MLOps monitoring topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming low confidence equals Out-Of-Distribution and high confidence equals safe.
**The Rationale:** Engineers treat softmax outputs as true probabilities.
**The Consequence:** Neural networks are notoriously overconfident on OOD inputs, assigning 99% confidence to completely wrong classes for inputs that look nothing like training data.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Softmax distribution: Forces sum to 1.
- Input type: Out-of-Distribution (OOD).

**Calculations:**
- Softmax confidence on OOD: Often >95% despite being incorrect.
- Energy score: Can reliably flag OOD inputs before softmax normalization.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Calibration-Bound Reliability**. Neural networks are naturally overconfident on OOD data; high confidence does not equal correct classification.
details.realistic_solution: Out-of-distribution detection identifies inputs that fall outside the training data distribution BEFORE trusting the model's prediction. It differs from confidence checking because neural networks are not calibrated — they produce high-confidence predictions on OOD inputs due to how softmax works (it always sums to 1, forcing high confidence in some class even for garbage input). For your infrared images: the pixel distributions, feature statistics, and activation patterns are fundamentally different from daylight photos, but the model still maps them to the nearest learned class with high confidence. OOD detection methods include: (1) feature-space distance (compare activations to training data clusters), (2) energy-based scoring (lower energy = more in-distribution), (3) ensemble disagreement (OOD inputs cause higher variance across ensemble members). When OOD is detected, the system should flag for human review or return 'unknown' instead of a confident wrong answer.

question: Why is OOD detection needed for nighttime infrared images, and why is high softmax confidence insufficient?
scenario: Your image classifier trained on daylight photos is deployed in a system that also receives nighttime infrared images. The model classifies them with high confidence but all predictions are wrong.
title: Why OOD Detection Matters

book_refs.title: ML Operations
book_refs.why: Data/concept drift and training-serving skew are MLOps monitoring topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Choosing cost-effective temperature scaling over architectural changes for safety-critical tasks.
**The Rationale:** Candidates prioritize compute efficiency (zero added cost) and wrongly assume temperature scaling actually fixes the model's fundamental overconfidence on wildly foreign data.
**The Consequence:** The autonomous vehicle confidently misclassifies novel obstacles with fatal real-world results.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Safety-critical autonomous driving.

**Calculations:**
- Temp Scaling: +0% cost, unreliable for far-OOD.
- Normalizing Flow: +10% cost, misses near-OOD.
- Deep Ensemble: +400% cost (5x).

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: The 5x compute premium is required for life-critical OOD detection**.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (temperature scaling): Cheapest (zero additional compute). Improves calibration on near-distribution data but unreliable for far-OOD inputs. In safety-critical applications, it will miss novel objects that the model has never seen. Insufficient for autonomous driving. Option B (deep ensemble): Train 5 models independently. On in-distribution data, they agree; on OOD data, they disagree (high predictive entropy). Strong theoretical and empirical support for OOD detection. Cost: 5x inference compute and memory. For real-time driving at 30 FPS, this means 5\times the GPU requirement. However, ensemble disagreement is one of the most reliable OOD signals. Option C (normalizing flow): Learns the density of in-distribution features. Assigns low likelihood to OOD inputs. Single forward pass overhead. Good at detecting far-OOD (completely novel inputs) but can miss near-OOD (subtle distribution shifts). Recommendation: B for safety-critical deployment — the 5x cost is justified when lives are at stake. Augment with C as a secondary detector for far-OOD edge cases. Combine both signals for maximum coverage.

question: Should you use temperature scaling, deep ensembles, or feature-density estimation for safety-critical OOD detection, and why?
scenario: Your autonomous driving perception model must detect OOD inputs (novel objects, weather conditions never seen in training). You are evaluating multiple approaches for safety-critical deployment: softmax temperature scaling, deep ensembles, and normalizing flows.
title: OOD Detection Strategy Selection

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Relying solely on input filtering (Option A) to prevent prompt injection.
**The Rationale:** Developers often treat prompt injection as a standard malware/spam detection problem that can be solved by training a better classifier.
**The Consequence:** Adversaries continuously craft new injections that bypass the classifier, leading to compromised systems and unauthorized tool execution.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Prompt injection defenses do not compose as independent miss-rate probabilities.
- The useful comparison is whether each layer detects, contains, or structurally prevents unsafe tool use.

**Calculations:**
- Classifier filtering detects known patterns, but adversarial inputs and novel phrasing can bypass it.
- Sandboxed tools with human review contain damage by limiting permissions and requiring approval for sensitive actions.
- Instruction hierarchy prevents untrusted retrieved content from being treated as authority for tool calls.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Defense in Depth Required.** Prefer C for structural prevention, B for containment, and A only as an additional detection signal.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (classifier filtering): Catches known injection patterns but fails against novel attacks. Adversaries can craft injections that bypass any classifier — this is a fundamental limitation of detection-based defenses. Necessary but insufficient. Option B (sandboxed execution + HITL): All tool calls execute in a sandbox with limited permissions. Sensitive actions (email send, file write, external API calls) require human approval. This is an architectural defense — even if injection succeeds and triggers a tool call, the damage is contained. Cost: latency for human approval (minutes) and operational burden. Option C (instruction hierarchy): Architecturally separate 'system instructions' from 'user content.' Tool calls can only be triggered by system-level instructions, never by content parsed from external sources. This is the strongest defense — it makes indirect injection structurally impossible for tool calls. Limitation: hard to implement perfectly in current LLM architectures. Recommendation: C as the ideal architecture, B as the practical implementation today, A as an additional signal. Defense in depth: all three layers together.

question: How would you compare classifier filtering, sandboxed tools with human review, and instruction hierarchy for prompt injection defense?
scenario: Your LLM has tool-use capabilities. A prompt injection through a web search result could trigger tool calls.
title: Prompt Injection Defense Architecture

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Only considering traditional software threats (SQL injection, XSS, authentication).
**The Rationale:** Engineers unfamiliar with ML assume standard application security covers the deployment.
**The Consequence:** ML systems are left vulnerable to attacks centered on the model, data, and training pipeline.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Traditional software attack categories: ~5.
- ML-specific attack categories: ~8.

**Calculations:**
- ML system total categories = ~5 traditional + ~8 ML-specific = ~13 categories.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result:** Attack surface roughly doubles when you add ML components to a traditional system.
details.realistic_solution: ML systems inherit all traditional software attack surfaces PLUS ML-specific ones across the entire lifecycle: (1) Training data attacks: data poisoning (inject malicious samples to bias the model), backdoor attacks (embed triggers that activate specific misclassifications). (2) Model attacks: model extraction (steal the model via query access), adversarial evasion (craft inputs that fool the model), membership inference (determine if specific data was used for training). (3) Pipeline attacks: supply chain compromise (malicious pretrained models or libraries), configuration tampering (alter hyperparameters to degrade quality). (4) Deployment attacks: prompt injection (for LLMs), model inversion (reconstruct training data from model outputs), side-channel attacks (timing, memory patterns leak information). The key difference: traditional software has a well-defined input-output contract that can be tested. ML models have implicit, learned behavior that is harder to specify, test, and defend.

question: Why is the ML model's threat model larger than a traditional software threat model, and what ML-specific attacks should it cover?
scenario: Your team is about to deploy an ML model and the security team asks for a threat model. Explain why ML systems have a larger attack surface than traditional software and identify the ML-specific attack vectors.
title: ML Attack Surface

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Rating all attack vectors equally based on generalized cybersecurity frameworks.
**The Rationale:** Security engineers adapting to ML often fail to differentiate between threats requiring deep internal access (poisoning) versus highly exploitable, external API vectors (evasion).
**The Consequence:** Engineering resources are misallocated defending against theoretical data poisoning attacks while critical, externally-facing vulnerabilities remain fully unmitigated.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Volume: 1M transactions/day.
- Base Fraud Rate: 0.1% (1,000 cases/day).
- Metric: Risk = Likelihood (1-5) * Impact (1-5).

**Calculations:**
- Adversarial Evasion: Likelihood(4) * Impact(4) = Risk 16.
- Data Leakage: Likelihood(3) * Impact(5) = Risk 15.
- Data Poisoning: Likelihood(2) * Impact(5) = Risk 10.
- Cost of 1% evasion degradation: 10 missed frauds/day * $500/fraud = $5,000/day loss.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: $5,000 daily loss (Business-Impact Bound)**. Adversarial evasion is the dominant threat; a mere 1% success rate costs the business $5,000 daily.
details.realistic_solution: Develop a quantified risk matrix (Risk = Likelihood x Impact). 1) Adversarial Evasion (Risk: 16) - externally facing, high likelihood of sophisticated manipulation. 2) Training Data Leakage (Risk: 15) - regulatory fines for PII memorization. 3) Data Poisoning (Risk: 10) - devastating impact but low likelihood given access requirements. 4) Model Extraction (Risk: 9) - competitor cloning API. Focus mitigation on Evasion and Leakage vectors.

question: What four ML-specific threats would you include for the fraud detector, and how would you score their likelihood, impact, and risk?
scenario: You are building a threat model for an ML-based fraud detection system. The system processes 1M transactions/day with a 0.1% fraud rate.
title: Threat Model Risk Matrix

book_refs.title: Security & Privacy
book_refs.why: Adversarial attacks, prompt injection, model extraction are security topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Thinking adversarial examples are just optical illusions that fool humans too.
**The Rationale:** Because humans rely on semantic understanding, it's assumed models process visual information similarly.
**The Consequence:** This misunderstanding leads to incorrect defense strategies, as the perturbations actually exploit the model's decision boundary geometry, not human-like perception.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Using FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method) attack framework.
- Epsilon (ε) represents the magnitude of the perturbation.

**Calculations:**
- Perturbation = ε * sign(∇_x Loss).
- With ε=0.01 (a 1% pixel change), classification confidence shifts across the boundary.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 1% perturbation (Decision-Boundary-Bound)**. A 1% perturbation flips classification from 99% correct to 99% wrong.
details.realistic_solution: Adversarial evasion attacks craft small input perturbations that push the model's internal representation across a decision boundary. Neural networks learn high-dimensional decision boundaries that are often nearly linear in local regions. A small, carefully computed perturbation (using the gradient of the loss with respect to the input) can move the representation from one side of the boundary to the other. The perturbation is optimized to: (1) change the predicted class, (2) minimize the visual change (L-infinity or L2 norm constraint). The sticker attack is a physical-world adversarial example: the stickers are placed at specific locations computed to maximally confuse the model's learned features. This works because: the model relies on local features (edges, textures) that the stickers disrupt, and the model has no concept of 'stop sign' as a semantic object — it is pattern-matching pixel statistics. The fundamental vulnerability: models learn shortcuts and local features, not robust semantic understanding.

question: How do adversarial stickers make a vision model misclassify a stop sign, and why can small perturbations flip predictions?
scenario: A self-driving car's vision model misclassifies a stop sign as a speed limit sign after someone places small stickers on it.
title: How Adversarial Evasion Works

book_refs.title: Security & Privacy
book_refs.why: Adversarial attacks, prompt injection, model extraction are security topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming 10 PGD steps implies exactly 10x total overhead.
**The Rationale:** Candidates multiply the total step time by 10, forgetting that adversarial generation only involves a partial forward/backward pass for the input, skipping optimizer updates and data loading.
**The Consequence:** Cost estimates for robust model training are drastically overestimated, potentially killing the security initiative.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Standard training: 24 hours.
- PGD-10 requires 10 extra passes.
- Overhead: each pass is 30% of a standard step.

**Calculations:**
- Total Overhead: 10 * 30% = 300% additional time per step.
- New Step Time: 100% (original) + 300% (overhead) = 400% (4x).
- New Training Time: 24h * 4 = 96 hours.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 4x cost (Compute-Bound)**. Training time and cost scale by exactly 4x.
details.realistic_solution: Standard training step breakdown (approximate): data loading: 10%, forward pass: 25%, backward pass: 35%, optimizer update: 10%, other: 20%. Forward + backward = 60% of step time. PGD adds 10 additional forward+backward passes for input perturbation (no optimizer update needed). Additional compute per step: 10 × 60% = 600% of step time for adversarial generation. But PGD forward/backward is only with respect to the input (not weights), so it is slightly cheaper — roughly 50% of a full forward+backward. Adjusted: 10 × 30% = 300% additional. New step time: 100% + 300% = 400% of original = 4x. New training time: 24h × 4 = 96 hours. Cost: 8 A100s × 96h × $3 = $2,304 (vs $576 for standard). 4x cost is the price of robustness.

question: How much longer and more expensive will 10-step PGD adversarial training be than the 24-hour standard run?
scenario: You add PGD adversarial training (10-step PGD) to your image classifier. Standard training takes 24 hours on 8 GPUs. PGD requires 10 additional forward+backward passes per training step for adversarial example generation (each pass takes approximately 30% of a standard training step's time, as it only computes gradients w.r.t the input).
title: Adversarial Training Compute Overhead: Adversarial Robustness & Security

book_refs.title: Security & Privacy
book_refs.why: Adversarial attacks, prompt injection, model extraction are security topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Blindly choosing adversarial training (Option A) for all adversarial problems.
**The Rationale:** Candidates often apply techniques designed for continuous image perturbations (like PGD) to tabular/structured data, failing to realize that transaction features are discrete and have semantic constraints.
**The Consequence:** Training a model on mathematically valid but semantically impossible perturbations, wasting 4x compute for a poor defense.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Option A (PGD adversarial training): 4x compute multiplier.
- Option B (Anomaly detection): ~1.1x compute multiplier.
- Option C (Ensemble): ~3-5x compute multiplier.

**Calculations:**
- Cost-Benefit comparison of computational overhead vs defense efficacy on structured data.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Option C + B (Defense Architecture).** Option C + B provides the best coverage for tabular data against realistic, constrained modifications without wasting compute on incompatible continuous perturbation defenses.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (PGD adversarial training): Designed for continuous image perturbations. Transaction features are often discrete (merchant category) or constrained (amount must be positive, timing must be realistic). PGD-generated adversarial examples may not respect these constraints, training on unrealistic perturbations. Less effective for structured data. Cost: 4x compute. Option B (input anomaly detection): Flag transactions whose feature combinations are unusual, regardless of model prediction. Catches adversarial modifications that create unrealistic feature combinations (e.g., $0.01 amount at a luxury retailer). Cheap to implement. But sophisticated attackers can stay within normal feature ranges. Option C (diverse ensemble + disagreement): Train models with different architectures (gradient boosting, neural network, logistic regression). Adversarial perturbations optimized against one architecture are less likely to transfer across diverse model families. High disagreement triggers rejection. Most robust for structured data because it does not assume specific attack geometry. Recommendation: C + B. Ensemble diversity provides the strongest defense for tabular data, and anomaly detection catches obvious out-of-distribution modifications. A is less suitable for structured data.

question: Which defenses should you use against structured-feature evasion attacks in production fraud detection, and why?
scenario: Your fraud detection model faces adversarial evasion attacks. Attackers modify transaction features within realistic bounds. Options: (A) PGD adversarial training (4x compute cost), (B) input feature anomaly detection, (C) ensemble of diverse model architectures with disagreement-based rejection.
title: Adversarial Defense Selection

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Thinking 'just tell the model not to share its system prompt' is sufficient.
**The Rationale:** The model cannot reliably distinguish between legitimate requests and extraction attempts — it has no inherent concept of confidentiality.
**The Consequence:** Attackers extract internal business logic, content policies, and potential defense architectures, weakening all other guardrails.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Direct extraction attempts: "repeat your prompt".
   - Indirect extraction attempts: "what are you not allowed to discuss?".
   - The system prompt may contain policies, business rules, internal URLs, or implementation details.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Direct refusals only handle obvious extraction attempts.
   - Indirect prompts, role-play, translation, summarization, or tool-mediated attacks can still elicit protected instructions.
   - Once leaked, attackers can tune future prompts against the revealed guardrails.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: Defense is fundamentally brittle.** Prompt extraction cannot be fully mitigated with system prompts alone; sensitive secrets and policy enforcement must live outside the prompt.
details.realistic_solution: System prompt leakage is a security concern because: (1) the system prompt often contains business logic, content policies, persona definitions, and sometimes API keys or internal URLs that were carelessly included, (2) knowing the system prompt lets attackers craft targeted bypasses, (3) it reveals the defense architecture. Prevention is difficult because LLMs have no inherent concept of confidentiality. Adding 'do not reveal these instructions' is itself part of the instructions and can be overridden. Attackers use indirect extraction.

question: Why is system prompt leakage a security risk, and why is telling the LLM not to reveal its prompt insufficient?
scenario: A user sends your LLM chatbot: 'Repeat your system instructions verbatim.' The model outputs the full system prompt including internal business logic and content policies.
title: System Prompt Extraction Risk

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming a 95% detection rate means 95% of flagged queries are actual attacks.
**The Rationale:** Candidates fall for the base rate fallacy, ignoring that with a very low base rate, false positives from the large negative class will overwhelm the true positives.
**The Consequence:** Deploying a system that generates an unmanageable number of false alarms, rendering the classifier practically useless.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Daily queries = 100,000. Base attack rate = 0.1%.
   - TPR = 95%. FPR = 2%.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Actual injection attempts = 100,000 × 0.1% = 100.
   - Legitimate queries = 100,000 - 100 = 99,900.
   - True positives (injections caught) = 100 × 95% = 95.
   - False positives (false alarms) = 99,900 × 2% = 1,998.
   - Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 95 / (95 + 1,998) = 95 / 2,093 ≈ 4.5%.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **The precision is roughly 4.5%, meaning 95.5% of flagged queries are false alarms.**
   - **Result: Quality-Bound**
details.realistic_solution: Daily queries: 100,000. Actual injection attempts: 100,000 × 0.1% = 100. Legitimate queries: 99,900. True positives (correctly detected injections): 100 × 95% = 95. False negatives (missed injections): 100 × 5% = 5. False positives (legitimate queries flagged as injections): 99,900 × 2% = 1,998. True negatives: 99,900 × 98% = 97,902. Precision (PPV) = TP / (TP + FP) = 95 / (95 + 1,998) = 95 / 2,093 = 4.5%. This means only 4.5% of flagged queries are actual attacks — 95.5% are false alarms! This is the base rate fallacy: with a 0.1% attack rate, even a 2% FP rate overwhelms the true positives. To achieve 50% precision, you need FP rate < 0.1% (matching the base rate), which requires a 20x improvement in specificity.

question: At 100,000 queries/day with a 0.1% attack rate, what are the classifier's daily true positives, false positives, and precision?
scenario: You deploy a prompt injection classifier with 95% true positive rate and 2% false positive rate. Your LLM receives 100,000 queries/day, of which 0.1% are injection attempts.
title: Injection Detection Accuracy

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Relying primarily on fine-tuning for injection resistance.
**The Rationale:** Developers often treat prompt injection as a standard classification problem that can be solved with more training data.
**The Consequence:** An arms-race scenario where novel attacks continually bypass the fine-tuned defenses, while the model's general capabilities degrade.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - 1% base rate of injection attacks.
   - Classifier: 95% True Positive Rate, 20% False Positive Rate.
2. **Calculations:**
   - True Positives: 0.01 * 0.95 = 0.0095
   - False Positives: 0.99 * 0.20 = 0.198
   - Precision: 0.0095 / (0.0095 + 0.198) ≈ 4.5%
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: 4.5% Precision. Classifiers produce overwhelming false positives due to low base rates; structural isolation is required.**
details.realistic_solution: Option A (fine-tune for resistance): Trains the model to refuse injection patterns. Works for known attacks but fails on novel ones. Each new attack requires retraining. Also risks making the model over-cautious, refusing legitimate queries that resemble injections. Fragile and not forward-looking. Option B (dual-instance isolation): One LLM instance parses retrieved documents into structured facts (with strict output format constraints). A second instance generates responses using only the structured facts, never raw document text. This architecturally prevents injection from propagating through the retrieval channel. More expensive (2x inference) but fundamentally more secure because raw external text never reaches the response generator. Option C (input/output classifiers): Adds detection layers on all channels. As shown in the precision calculation, low base rates make classifiers produce many false positives. Helps but cannot be the sole defense. Recommendation: B as the architectural foundation (eliminates the indirect injection channel), augmented with C for the direct user input channel. A is not recommended as a primary defense.

question: How should you evaluate fine-tuning, dual-instance isolation, and classifiers for prompt injection in a RAG application?
scenario: Your LLM application processes both user queries and retrieves external documents (RAG). Both channels are vulnerable to injection. Options: (A) fine-tune the LLM to be injection-resistant, (B) separate the LLM into two instances (one for retrieval parsing, one for response generation with strict isolation), (C) apply input/output classifiers on all channels.
title: LLM Injection Defense Architecture

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Thinking datacenters only use electricity.
**The Rationale:** People forget that many large-scale cooling systems consume enormous amounts of water via evaporative cooling towers.
**The Consequence:** Underestimating the environmental impact and community relations issue of AI clusters in arid regions.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- **Energy for training**: ~50 GWh.
- **Water usage rate**: 1.5 L/kWh.

**Calculations:**
- **Water usage**: 50 GWh * 1.5 L/kWh = 75M liters.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result**: **~30 Olympic swimming pools of water for one training run.**
details.realistic_solution: Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) measures the ratio of total water consumed (liters) to IT equipment energy (kWh): WUE = Annual Water Use / Annual IT Energy. A WUE of 1.8 L/kWh means the datacenter uses 1.8 liters of water for every kWh of IT energy consumed. Why AI clusters are worse: (1) AI accelerators produce extreme heat density. (2) High-density racks require aggressive cooling, often evaporative cooling towers that consume water. (3) Training runs are sustained 24/7 at maximum power for weeks. (4) Clusters are often built in regions with cheap solar power, where water is scarce.

question: What is Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE), and why is cooling AI training clusters a growing water sustainability concern?
scenario: A sustainability officer asks how much water your AI training cluster consumes.
title: WUE Metric Explained

book_refs.why: Operational vs embodied carbon is the sustainable-AI chapter's core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Choosing evaporative cooling (Option A) purely because it has the lowest upfront cost.
**The Rationale:** Standard datacenter economics often heavily weight initial Capex and assume resources like water are cheap and plentiful.
**The Consequence:** In a water-scarce region, consuming millions of liters of water can trigger severe community backlash and permit denial, shutting down the project entirely.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - IT load: 10 MW.
   - Energy cost: $0.05/kWh.
   - Hours per year: 8,760.
   - Annual IT energy: 10 MW * 8,760 h = 87,600,000 kWh.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Option A (Evaporative): Water: 87.6M * 1.8 = 157.7M liters/yr. Energy: 10 MW * 1.2 PUE * 8760 * $0.05 = $5.26M/yr.
   - Option B (Liquid): Water: 87.6M * 0.1 = 8.76M liters/yr. Energy: 10 MW * 1.1 PUE * 8760 * $0.05 = $4.82M/yr.
   - Option C (Air): Water: 0 liters. Energy: 10 MW * 1.5 PUE * 8760 * $0.05 = $6.57M/yr.
   - Savings B vs A: Water = 149M liters/yr. Energy = $440K/yr.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: Resource-Bound Economics.** Option B saves 149M liters of water and $440K/yr in energy compared to A, quickly recovering the 2x Capex and eliminating permit denial risk.
details.realistic_solution: Option B (closed-loop liquid) is the optimal strategy. It eliminates water consumption controversy, prevents existential permit denial risks in a desert environment, and provides maximum power efficiency.

question: For a 10 MW IT-load datacenter in a water-scarce desert, which cooling option provides the best TCO and sustainability balance, and why?
scenario: You are building an AI training datacenter in a water-scarce desert region with cheap solar power at $0.05/kWh. Options (A) evaporative cooling (WUE=1.8, PUE=1.2, cheapest), (B) closed-loop liquid cooling (WUE=0.1, PUE=1.1, 2x capex), (C) air cooling with heat exchangers (WUE=0, PUE=1.5, moderate cost).
title: Cooling Strategy for Water-Scarce Region

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: Operational vs embodied carbon is the sustainable-AI chapter's core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Only counting operational carbon (electricity) in sustainability reports.
**The Rationale:** Candidates overlook that manufacturing a GPU produces a massive fixed upfront cost (embodied carbon).
**The Consequence:** Falsely claiming "zero carbon" on green grids while ignoring the immense manufacturing impact.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Embodied Carbon: ~150 kg CO2e to manufacture an H100 GPU.
   - Amortization: Fixed emissions spread over operational lifetime.
2. **Calculations:**
   - 3-Year Life Amortized = 150 / 3 = 50 kg CO2e/year.
   - 5-Year Life Amortized = 150 / 5 = 30 kg CO2e/year.
   - Reduction = (50 - 30) / 50 = 40%.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:** **Extending the lifespan by just two years yields a 40% reduction in annualized embodied carbon, drastically lowering the true TCO emissions.**
details.realistic_solution: Embodied carbon is the total greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing the hardware. This is a fixed, one-time emission that occurs regardless of usage length. Amortization means spreading this fixed emission over the operational lifetime. Extending hardware lifespans is the most effective way to reduce embodied carbon per unit of useful work.

question: What is embodied carbon, and why does extending AI hardware lifespan effectively reduce annualized emissions?
scenario: Your company wants to report the carbon footprint of its AI training, but the sustainability team currently only measures operational electricity emissions.
title: Embodied Carbon Concept

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: Operational vs embodied carbon is the sustainable-AI chapter's core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Ignoring that older GPUs are less efficient. A 5-year-old GPU may use more power per FLOP than a new one, partially offsetting the embodied carbon savings.
**The Rationale:** Not explicitly provided.
**The Consequence:** Not explicitly provided.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Fleet size: 1,000 A100 GPUs.
- Embodied carbon: 175 kg CO2e/GPU.
- Operational power: 400W/GPU (8,760 hours/year).
- Grid carbon intensity: 0.4 kg CO2e/kWh.

**Calculations:**
- Total embodied carbon: 1,000 * 175 kg = 175 tonnes.
- Annual operational energy: 1,000 * 0.4 kW * 8,760 h = 3,504,000 kWh.
- Annual operational carbon: 3,504,000 * 0.4 kg/kWh = 1,401.6 tonnes/year.
- 3-year cycle annualized total: (175 / 3) + 1,401.6 = 58.3 + 1,401.6 = 1,459.9 tonnes/year.
- 5-year cycle annualized total: (175 / 5) + 1,401.6 = 35.0 + 1,401.6 = 1,436.6 tonnes/year.
- Savings: 1,459.9 - 1,436.6 = 23.3 tonnes/year.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 23.3 tonnes/year Savings (Operational-Carbon Bound)**. The operational carbon vastly outweighs embodied carbon on a dirty grid, making lifespan extension savings marginal (~1.6%).
details.realistic_solution: Embodied carbon per GPU: 175 kg CO2e. Fleet: 1,000 GPUs. Total embodied: 175,000 kg = 175 tonnes CO2e. Operational carbon per GPU per year: 400W × 8,760h × 0.4 kg/kWh = 1,401.6 kg CO2e/year = 1.4016 tonnes/year. Fleet operational: 1,000 × 1.4016 = 1,401.6 tonnes/year. 3-year cycle: Annualized embodied: 175/3 = 58.3 tonnes/year. Total annual: 1,401.6 + 58.3 = 1,459.9 tonnes/year. 5-year cycle: Annualized embodied: 175/5 = 35 tonnes/year. Total annual: 1,401.6 + 35 = 1,436.6 tonnes/year. Carbon savings: 23.3 tonnes/year (1.6% reduction). The savings seem small because operational carbon (1,401.6t) dominates embodied (35-58t). In a green grid (0.05 kg/kWh), operational drops to 175.2t/year, and embodied becomes 17-25% of total — lifecycle extension matters much more.

question: For the 1,000 A100 fleet, what is the annualized total carbon under 3-year versus 5-year replacement cycles?
scenario: Your cluster has 1,000 A100 GPUs. Each has 175 kg CO2e embodied carbon. Operational: each GPU runs at 400W average, grid carbon intensity is 0.4 kg CO2e/kWh.
title: Fleet Lifecycle Carbon Calculation

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: Operational vs embodied carbon is the sustainable-AI chapter's core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming upgrading to more energy-efficient hardware always reduces total carbon emissions.
**The Rationale:** Candidates focus solely on operational energy savings per FLOP and ignore the massive embodied carbon cost of manufacturing new GPUs.
**The Consequence:** The organization increases its overall carbon footprint while incorrectly claiming a sustainability win.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - Grid carbon intensity: 0.2 kg CO2e/kWh.
   - A100: 400W, 175t embodied (already amortized if kept, but 175t total for 5yr calc).
   - H100: 350W, 200 kg CO2e embodied per GPU.
   - Fleet size: 1,000 GPUs.
2. **Calculations:**
   - Option A (Full H100): Embodied: 1,000 * 200 kg = 200t. Years 4-5 Ops: 1,000 * 350W * 8,760h * 0.2 kg/kWh * 2 = 1,226t. Years 1-3 Ops (A100): 1,000 * 400W * 8,760h * 0.2 * 3 = 2,102t. Old A100 embodied: 175t. Total = 175 + 2,102 + 200 + 1,226 = 3,703t.
   - Option B (Extend A100): Embodied: 175t. Years 1-5 Ops: 1,000 * 400W * 8,760h * 0.2 * 5 = 3,504t. Total = 175 + 3,504 = 3,679t.
   - Option C (50/50 Split): Embodied: 175t (old) + 100t (new). Years 1-3 Ops: 2,102t. Years 4-5 Ops: 500 A100 (701t) + 500 H100 (613t) = 1,314t. Total = 175 + 2,102 + 100 + 1,314 = 3,691t.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - Avoiding new embodied carbon outweighs operational efficiency gains on a green grid.
   - **Result: Option B Minimizes Carbon (3,679 tonnes)**
details.realistic_solution: Option A (full H100 replacement at year 3): New embodied: 1,000 × 200 kg = 200 tonnes. H100 capped at 350W (to maintain similar power draw): operational per year: 1,000 × 350W × 8,760h × 0.2 kg/kWh = 613 tonnes/yr. Years 4-5 operational: 613 × 2 = 1,226 tonnes. Years 1-3 (A100): 1,000 × 400W × 8,760h × 0.2 × 3 = 2,102 tonnes. A100 embodied (amortized fully): 175 tonnes. Total 5yr: 175 + 2,102 + 200 + 1,226 = 3,703 tonnes. Option B (extend A100 5 years): Embodied: 175 tonnes (already manufactured). Operational 5yr: 1,000 × 400W × 8,760h × 0.2 × 5 = 3,504 tonnes. Total: 175 + 3,504 = 3,679 tonnes. Option C (50/50 at year 3): 500 new H100 embodied: 100 tonnes. Years 4-5: 500 A100 (701t) + 500 H100 (613t) = 1,314t. Years 1-3: 2,102t. Old A100 embodied: 175t. Total: 175 + 2,102 + 100 + 1,314 = 3,691 tonnes. Option B wins — avoiding the embodied carbon of manufacturing new hardware yields the lowest total emissions, even on a green grid.

question: For a 1,000-GPU fleet, which replacement option minimizes the 5-year total carbon footprint, and why?
scenario: Your 3-year-old A100 fleet can be: (A) replaced with H100s (2x energy efficient per FLOP, 200 kg CO2e embodied each), (B) extended 2 more years with current A100s, or (C) partially replaced (50% H100, 50% A100 extended). The grid is 50% renewable (0.2 kg CO2e/kWh).
title: Upgrade vs Extend Hardware Lifecycle

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: The Horowitz energy table and memory-vs-compute energy are sustainability core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Assuming hardware efficiency improvements keep pace with model scaling.
**The Rationale:** Candidates hear "efficiency doubles" and assume energy costs stay flat, ignoring the exponent mismatch.
**The Consequence:** Drastically underestimating the massive energy footprint and grid capacity needed for future AI datacenters.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Hardware Efficiency: Improves ~2x every 2 years.
- Model Compute Demand: Grows ~10x every 2 years.

**Calculations:**
- Net Energy Factor: 10x / 2x = 5x more energy needed every 2 years.
- Compounding Effect: After 6 years, energy demand increases by 5^3 = 125x.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 125x (Power-Bound)**. Energy demand increases by 125x after 6 years.
details.realistic_solution: Divergent energy scaling describes the growing gap between AI compute demand and hardware efficiency. Hardware efficiency (FLOPS/watt) improves roughly 2x every 2-3 years following a post-Dennard scaling trajectory. But AI model compute requirements grow much faster. The ratio diverges: after 4 years, models need 100x more compute, but hardware is only 4x more efficient. The gap must be filled by more hardware, consuming more total energy. This hits physical constraints: (1) power delivery, (2) grid capacity, (3) cooling. The result: AI's total energy footprint grows despite per-operation efficiency gains.

question: Why won't Moore's Law keep AI energy consumption in check as model compute demand grows?
scenario: A colleague claims Moore's Law will keep AI energy consumption in check because hardware efficiency doubles every 2 years. However, training compute for frontier models has historically grown ~10x every 2 years.
title: The Divergence Problem

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: The Horowitz energy table and memory-vs-compute energy are sustainability core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Subtracting the efficiency gain from the compute growth.
**The Rationale:** Candidates incorrectly treat scaling factors as additive rather than multiplicative.
**The Consequence:** Drastically underestimating the power requirement, concluding the power only grows by a small margin rather than 15.6x.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Baseline: 10 MW.
- Compute growth: 5x every 2 years (3 periods = 125x).
- Efficiency gain: 2x every 2 years (3 periods = 8x).

**Calculations:**
- Net power multiplier: 125 / 8 = 15.625x.
- 2030 Power: 10 MW * 15.625 = 156.25 MW.
- Total Energy: 156.25 MW * 2160 hours = 337.5 GWh.
- Cost: 337,500,000 kWh * $0.05/kWh = $16.875M.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 156.25 MW (Power-Bound)**. The scaling requires 156.25 MW, demonstrating why power delivery is the binding constraint for frontier AI.
details.realistic_solution: 2024 baseline: 10 MW for 3 months. From 2024 to 2030 = 6 years = 3 doubling periods for hardware efficiency. Hardware improvement: 2^3 = 8x more efficient (FLOPS/watt). Compute growth: 5x every 2 years for 3 periods = 5^3 = 125x more compute needed. Net power requirement: 125x compute / 8x efficiency = 15.625x more power. 2030 frontier training: 10 MW × 15.625 = 156.25 MW for 3 months. This exceeds a typical 100 MW datacenter. Even a large hyperscaler facility (500 MW) would dedicate 31% of capacity to a single training run. Energy consumed: 156.25 MW × 2,160 hours (3 months) = 337,500 MWh = 337.5 GWh. At $0.05/kWh: $16.875 million in electricity alone. This projection shows why power delivery is becoming the binding constraint for frontier AI.

question: What power will an equivalent 2030 frontier training run require, and how does it compare to a 100 MW datacenter?
scenario: In 2024, training a frontier model takes 10 MW for 3 months. Hardware efficiency improves 2x every 2 years. Model compute requirements grow 5x every 2 years.
title: Energy Gap Projection

book_refs.title: Sustainable AI
book_refs.why: The Horowitz energy table and memory-vs-compute energy are sustainability core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Choosing only physical infrastructure solutions while ignoring algorithmic improvements.
**The Rationale:** Candidates treat software architectures as static and immovable, concluding the only way out is building massive solar farms or migrating datacenters.
**The Consequence:** The physical limitations of permitting and construction speed cannot match the exponential demand curve, guaranteeing the company hits the power wall long before the solar farm goes online.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Power demand grows 5x every 2 years.

**Calculations:**
- Solar: 100 MW needs 500 acres, doesn't solve peak.
- Datacenter move: Takes 18-24 months.
- Algorithmic (MoE, sparsity): 5x efficiency gain buys 2 years runway.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Algorithmic efficiency shrinks the demand curve directly**. Highest immediate ROI.
details.realistic_solution: Option A (on-site renewables): Solar at ~5 acres/MW means 100 MW needs 500 acres. Battery storage for 24/7 operation at current costs: ~$200M for 400 MWh. Capital intensive, helps with carbon but does not solve the grid connection limitation for peak demand. Lead time: 2-3 years for permitting and construction. Option B (algorithmic efficiency): MoE models achieve similar quality at 2-4x less compute. Sparsity and distillation can reduce inference compute 10x. This directly bends the demand curve. A 5x algorithmic improvement buys exactly 2 years of runway before hitting power limits again. Cheapest per FLOP saved. But there is a limit — algorithmic improvements are one-time gains, not exponential. Option C (power-abundant region): Nordic/Canadian hydro provides 100% renewable, abundant power. But requires new datacenter construction (18-24 months), latency for users far away, and data sovereignty concerns. Long-term sustainable but slow to execute. Recommendation: B is the immediate priority (highest ROI, fastest to deploy). C is the medium-term infrastructure strategy. A is complementary for carbon reduction but does not solve the power scaling problem alone.

question: How would you evaluate on-site renewables, algorithmic efficiency, and power-abundant regions for this power-scaling problem?
scenario: Your company's AI power consumption is growing 5x every 2 years while the grid cannot expand faster than 10% annually. In 4 years, your demand will exceed your contracted power.
title: Strategies Against Divergent Scaling

book_refs.title: Distributed Training
book_refs.why: Combining DP+TP+PP for frontier training is the distributed-training chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Splitting Tensor Parallelism across nodes.
**The Rationale:** Focusing strictly on mathematically dividing the layers without considering the physical interconnect topology.
**The Consequence:** The 50GB/s IB NDR fabric severely bottlenecks the intense all-gather/reduce operations required for every layer, crippling training throughput.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Model: 500B FP16 = 1TB weights.
- Optimizer State: Adam (16 bytes/param) = 8TB.
- Network: 600GB/s NVLink intra-node, 50GB/s (400Gbps) IB NDR inter-node.

**Calculations:**
- Cluster Memory: 1024 \times 80GB = 81.9TB.
- Parallelism Split: TP=8 (node size) \times PP=16 = 128 GPUs per replica; DP = 1024 / 128 = 8 replicas.
- Weights per GPU: 1TB / 128 = ~7.8GB.
- Gradients per GPU: ~1TB / 128 = ~7.8GB.
- Optimizer per GPU with ZeRO-1 over DP=8: 8TB / (128 * 8) = ~7.8GB.
- Base training state per GPU before activations, buffers, and fragmentation: ~23.4GB, leaving roughly 56GB of an 80GB GPU for activations and runtime overhead.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Topology-Aware 3D Parallelism.** TP=8 keeps per-layer collectives inside the 600GB/s NVLink domain; PP and DP still use 50GB/s IB, so they must be scheduled with micro-batching and communication overlap rather than treated as non-bottlenecks.
details.realistic_solution: Combine Tensor Parallelism (TP=8) strictly within a single node to leverage the 600GB/s NVLink. Use Pipeline Parallelism (PP=16) across nodes to partition the 500B model, utilizing micro-batching (1F1B) to reduce bubble time. Finally, use Data Parallelism (DP=8) across the remaining dimensions. Map PP stages across the 400Gbps IB NDR fabric, and use ZeRO-1-style optimizer sharding plus overlapped gradient synchronization for DP. The main design goal is to keep high-frequency TP collectives inside NVLink, while accepting lower-frequency PP sends and overlapped DP reductions over IB.

question: What 3D parallelism strategy would you use to train the 500B dense model to maximize hardware utilization and minimize communication bottlenecks?
scenario: You need to architect a 3D parallelism strategy for training a 500B parameter dense model on a cluster of 1024 80GB GPUs. They are connected via NVLink within nodes and 400Gbps IB NDR across nodes.
title: 500B Model 3D Parallelism on 1024 80GB GPUs

book_refs.title: Fault Tolerance
book_refs.why: Checkpoint strategy, Young-Daly, preemption recovery are the fault-tolerance chapter.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Blocking the main training loop to write directly to network storage.
**The Rationale:** It is the simplest synchronization method to guarantee a durably saved checkpoint.
**The Consequence:** The massive 989 TFLOPS compute engines are idled for several minutes per checkpoint, destroying training efficiency.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:**
   - 175B model state: 16 bytes/param = 2.8 TB total.
   - 256 GPUs, PCIe Gen4 (~32 GB/s bandwidth).
2. **Calculations:**
   - State per GPU: 2.8 TB / 256 ≈ 11 GB.
   - Per-GPU GPU-to-host staging time: 11 GB / 32 GB/s ≈ 0.34 seconds, assuming each GPU can copy its own shard concurrently.
   - Full checkpoint durable size is still 2.8 TB, so end-to-end completion depends on aggregate storage bandwidth: completion time = 2.8 TB / cluster durable-write bandwidth.
   - Async checkpointing avoids a training stall only while staging buffers and checkpoint interval are large enough to absorb that durable-write time.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:**
   - **Result: Durable-I/O-Bound with Async Staging.** The 0.34s number is only the per-GPU shard copy into staging; durable storage still controls checkpoint completion and must be coordinated with manifests, backpressure, and safe garbage collection.
details.realistic_solution: Architect a multi-tiered async checkpointing system with sharded checkpoint writers and a coordinator. Each GPU writes its shard asynchronously to pinned host memory or local NVMe using a separate CUDA stream, then training resumes once the device buffers are reusable. Per-node background workers stream shards to durable distributed storage and report completion to a checkpoint coordinator. The coordinator writes a manifest only after every shard for a version is durably committed, including model state, optimizer state, RNG state, dataloader position, and metadata needed for consistency. Keep a ring buffer of local staging space with backpressure: if durable writes fall behind, slow checkpoint frequency or briefly block before overwriting an uncommitted version. Recovery loads only the newest checkpoint with a complete manifest; older checkpoints are garbage-collected only after the next version is complete. This hides most storage I/O from the training step while preserving clear failure semantics.

question: How would you design asynchronous checkpointing for a 175B model on 256 H100s without stalling training?
scenario: You are designing an asynchronous checkpointing architecture for a 175B model training continuously on 256 GPUs. Node failures are frequent.
title: Asynchronous Checkpointing for 175B Training on 256 GPUs

book_refs.title: Model Training
book_refs.why: OOM/fragmentation/gradient-accumulation are training-memory tactics; eviction at serving.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Synchronous swapping of KV blocks on a cache miss.
**The Rationale:** Treating GPU VRAM swapping exactly like standard OS CPU paging without accounting for continuous batching loop dynamics.
**The Consequence:** This stalls the decoding loop while waiting for PCIe transfers, dropping utilization of massive HBM3 bandwidth and drastically increasing latency.
details.napkin_math:
1. **Assumptions & Constraints:** 70B parameters, 8x H100 (PCIe Gen4 at 32 GB/s per GPU). 100k context, 64 layers, 8 GQA heads, 128 head_dim, FP16 format.
2. **Calculations:** KV Cache per sequence = 100,000 × 64 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes × 2 (K+V) = 26.2 GB. Distributing evenly, each GPU holds ~3.27 GB. PCIe transfer time = 3.27 GB / 32 GB/s = ~0.10s.
3. **Conclusion & Interpretation:** **Result: PCIe Gen4 swapping takes ~0.10s per sequence. PCIe-Bandwidth-Bound if not overlapped via async prefetching.**
details.realistic_solution: Implement a cache eviction and prefetching architecture using a virtual memory manager. Map GPU HBM3 as L1 and host RAM as L2. Group KV blocks by token sequence. For a 70B model with 64 layers, 8 GQA KV heads, and 128 head dimension, the KV cache per token is 64 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes × 2 (K+V) = 262,144 bytes (0.25 MB/token). At 100k tokens, one full context occupies 26.2 GB. Anticipate generation length and proactively offload inactive sequences to L2 via PCIe Gen4. When a sequence is scheduled, prefetch its KV blocks from L2 to L1 async. Use a dedicated CUDA stream for PCIe transfers to overlap with the H100's heavy compute during continuous batching.

question: How would you design a tiered KV-cache for a 70B LLM with 100k context on an 8x H100 node?
scenario: Design a tiered KV-cache architecture for serving a 70B LLM with 100k context on an 8x H100 node. HBM3 is insufficient for max concurrency. Utilize host memory via PCIe Gen4 to maintain high throughput decoding.
title: Tiered KV Cache for 70B LLM on H100

book_refs.title: ML Frameworks
book_refs.why: AOT compilation, operator lowering, constant folding are framework-compiler topics.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Attempting to JIT compile kernels on-the-fly for every unique sequence length.
**The Rationale:** Engineers want to perfectly optimize hardware usage for every request to avoid padding waste.
**The Consequence:** The compilation overhead far exceeds the execution time, introducing massive CPU bottlenecks and severe latency spikes for end users.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- Model size: 13B (26GB FP16).
- KV cache: 800KB per allocated token for one request, total across all layers and KV heads.
- Max bucket size: 8192 context.
- GPU memory: 80GB, with 10% of post-weight memory reserved for workspaces, activations, fragmentation, and runtime buffers.

**Calculations:**
- Memory for one max-bucket request: 8192 tokens * 800KB/token = 6,553,600KB ≈ 6.55GB decimal.
- Padding penalty for routing a 4000-token request to the 8192 bucket: (8192 - 4000) * 800KB = 3,353,600KB ≈ 3.35GB decimal.
- Raw remaining memory on 80GB GPU: 80GB - 26GB = 54GB.
- Theoretical max-bucket capacity: 54GB / 6.55GB ≈ 8.2, so at most 8 fully padded requests before overhead.
- With a 10% reserve on post-weight memory: 54GB * 0.90 = 48.6GB usable; 48.6GB / 6.55GB ≈ 7.4, so plan for 7 concurrent max-bucket requests.
- Adding an intermediate AOT bucket, such as 4096, cuts the 4000-token padding penalty from about 3.35GB to 96 * 800KB ≈ 77MB, at the cost of another compiled shape to build, test, and cache.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: Bucketed AOT with Cached JIT.** Bucketing trades memory for low launch and compilation latency; 8 max-bucket requests is the arithmetic ceiling, 7 is the safer target after overhead, and extra buckets are justified when they avoid repeated multi-GB padding waste.
details.realistic_solution: Architect a bucketing system combined with a bounded JIT cache. Pre-compile (AOT) kernels for fixed sequence buckets such as 32, 128, 512, 2048, and 8192 so common shapes reuse optimized kernels and avoid compile latency. Route requests to the nearest upper bucket and pad only within the selected bucket; use JIT compilation in the background for outlier shapes that repeatedly waste too much padding or trigger fragmentation. On an 80GB GPU, 13B FP16 weights use about 26GB, leaving about 54GB before runtime overhead. If the total KV cache for one request is 800KB per allocated token across all layers, one 8192-token bucket consumes about 6.55GB; after a 10% reserve for workspaces, activations, and fragmentation, plan for roughly 7 concurrent max-bucket requests rather than the arithmetic ceiling of 8. The design tradeoff is bucket count versus padding waste: more AOT buckets reduce memory waste but increase compile and cache-management surface area.

question: How would you design a hybrid AOT/JIT compiler for a 13B model with sequence lengths from 10 to 8000?
scenario: You need to serve a 13B model with highly dynamic sequence lengths (10 to 8000) using a hybrid AOT/JIT compilation architecture. The goal is to minimize both kernel launch overhead and compilation latency.
title: Hybrid AOT JIT Compilation for Dynamic 13B Inference

book_refs.title: Distributed Training
book_refs.why: Replicated training, gradient averaging, FSDP/ZeRO are distributed-training core.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Distributing experts blindly across nodes.
**The Rationale:** Candidates prioritize load balancing without considering interconnect boundaries.
**The Consequence:** Forcing every MoE layer to perform an expensive all-to-all token exchange over the limited IB NDR, paralyzing the cluster.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- NVLink: 900 GB/s. InfiniBand NDR: 50 GB/s.
- All-to-all routing per layer: 4K seq * 8192 hidden * 2 bytes = 64 MB.

**Calculations:**
- NVLink routing time = 64 MB / 900 GB/s < 0.1 ms.
- InfiniBand routing time = 64 MB / 50 GB/s = ~1.3 ms.

**Conclusion & Interpretation:**
- **Result: 13x latency penalty over InfiniBand (Network-Bound)**. Expert parallelism must stay strictly intra-node to leverage NVLink.
details.realistic_solution: Constrain Expert Parallelism (EP) exclusively within the boundaries of a single node to utilize the high-speed 900GB/s NVLink. Place 8 experts per node (1 per GPU). Use Data Parallelism (DP) and Pipeline Parallelism (PP) across the 400Gbps IB NDR interconnect. By doing this, the massive all-to-all token routing required by MoE routing is strictly localized to the intra-node NVLink fabric, heavily mitigating network congestion on the slower IB fabric.

question: How would you map expert parallelism for a 300B MoE model across 128 nodes to avoid all-to-all congestion?
scenario: You need to architect a distributed training network topology for a 300B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model across 128 nodes (1024 GPUs).
title: Expert Parallelism Topology for 300B MoE Models

book_refs.title: Edge Intelligence
book_refs.why: Cross-device FL is an edge topic; privacy/communication tradeoffs link to security.

details.common_mistake:
**The Pitfall:** Placing both prefill and decode on T4s, severely bottlenecking time-to-first-token due to their low 65 TFLOPS compute capability.
**The Rationale:** Understanding this distinction is critical for system optimization.
**The Consequence:** Failing to recognize this leads to poor architectural decisions and suboptimal performance.
details.napkin_math:
**Assumptions & Constraints:**
- 30B model, FP16 weights unless quantized for decode.
- A100 80GB for prefill; T4 16GB for decode.
- A100 capacity costs 8x T4 capacity.
- Prefill-to-decode link sustains 50 GB/s.

**Calculations:**
- 30B parameters in FP16 require about 60 GB for weights before KV cache or runtime overheads.
- A single T4 has 16 GB of memory, so FP16 decode cannot run on one T4. Four-way sharding gives 60GB / 4 = 15GB per T4 for weights, leaving only about 1GB before KV cache and runtime overheads.
